books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”

primary_sources: Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832, 1832

stimulus.text:
After Nat Turner's rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia, in August 1831, the Virginia legislature debated ending slavery in the winter of 1831-1832. The debate failed, and Thomas R. Dew, a professor at the College of William and Mary, defended slavery in a pamphlet published in 1832:

“In the debate in the Virginia legislature, no speaker insinuated even, we believe that the slaves in Virginia were not treated kindly; and all too agreed that they were most abundantly fed, and we have no doubt but that they form the happiest portion of our society.”

“A merrier being does not exist on the face of the globe than the negro slave of the United States.”
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832 (1832), p. 66, as quoted in the Contemporary Argumentation and Debate account of Dew's pamphlet and in the Free Library account. Context checked against Digital History, University of Houston (ID 370).

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832 (1832), public domain
stem: In the passages, Dew argues that enslaved people in Virginia were what?

options.text: Plotting to rebel because their masters treated them cruelly
options.misconception: Dew says the opposite: he claims slaves were treated kindly and were happy.

options.text: Eager for the legislature to free them and send them to Africa
options.misconception: Dew argues against freeing enslaved people; he never says they wanted to leave.

options.text: Better off under slavery than free Black people in the North
options.misconception: The passages say nothing about free Black people in the North.

options.text: Well fed, kindly treated, and the happiest part of society

rationales.A: Dew says the opposite. He claims slaves were treated kindly and were happy.
rationales.B: Dew argues against freeing enslaved people. He never says they wanted to leave.
rationales.C: The passages say nothing about free Black people in the North.
rationales.D: Dew says all agreed the slaves were most abundantly fed, and he calls them the happiest portion of society and the merriest beings on earth.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first passage. Dew says no speaker claimed slaves were treated unkindly, and all agreed they were most abundantly fed.
2. Read the second. He calls the enslaved person the merriest being on earth.
3. Name the argument. Dew claims slavery made enslaved people happy, so it needs no apology.
Background: Dew wrote after the Virginia legislature debated ending slavery and decided to keep it.
Remember: a defense that praises a system is stronger than one that only excuses it.
